title: Feed Ranking & Real-Time
description: Explore EdgeRank-style feed ranking with affinity, weight, and decay signals, ML ranking pipelines, real-time push via WebSocket, content moderation, and Snowflake ID generation.

segments.text: Chronological feeds died at scale. When you follow a thousand accounts, a time-sorted feed shows you random noise. Facebook's EdgeRank — now deprecated but conceptually foundational — scored each story as affinity times weight times decay. The key insight: what users engage with matters more than when it was posted.

Affinity measures how close you are to the creator — do you message them, view their profile, react to their posts? Weight reflects the content type — videos score higher than text, comments score higher than likes. Decay penalizes old content exponentially. Multiply these three signals and you have a relevance score per story.

Modern ranking uses ML models with hundreds of features. The pipeline: candidate generation selects the top five hundred posts from your network, then a ranking model scores each one using features like past engagement, content freshness, creator reputation, and diversity signals. Facebook uses a deep learning model retrained daily on billions of engagement events.

Real-time feed updates use WebSocket connections. When your friend posts, the fan-out service pushes the new story to your active WebSocket connection. At Meta, each user has a persistent WebSocket connection to a presence server. With two billion daily active users, that's billions of concurrent connections managed by a fleet of edge servers.

Real-time push for celebrities is a problem. When someone with ten million followers posts, you need to push to ten million WebSocket connections. How do you handle this without overwhelming your push infrastructure?
segments.thought_prompt: How would you fan out a post from a celebrity with 10M followers in real-time without overwhelming the system?

segments.text: Content moderation runs in the write path. Before a post enters the fan-out pipeline, it passes through automated classifiers — hate speech, spam, nudity, violence. Facebook's moderation system makes over a million enforcement decisions per day. False positives remove legitimate content; false negatives let harmful content spread. The threshold is a business decision, not a technical one.

Twitter's Snowflake generates unique, time-sorted IDs without coordination. Sixty-four bits: forty-one bits for timestamp in milliseconds giving sixty-nine years of IDs, ten bits for machine ID giving one thousand and twenty-four machines, twelve bits for sequence giving four thousand and ninety-six IDs per millisecond per machine. IDs are sortable by creation time — perfect for feeds.

Feed diversity prevents filter bubbles. After ranking, apply diversity rules: no more than two posts from the same creator consecutively, mix content types — text, photos, videos — and include some exploration posts from accounts you don't follow. Instagram's Explore tab uses a separate ranking model optimized for discovery rather than engagement.

Every ranking change is A/B tested. Split users into control and treatment groups. Measure engagement metrics: time spent, likes, comments, shares. But also measure negative signals: 'hide post' clicks, unfollows, session abandonment. Instagram found that optimizing purely for engagement increased clickbait — they added quality signals to counterbalance.

Design the feed ranking pipeline for a social network with fifty million users and an average of five hundred posts per day per user in their network. Walk through candidate generation, scoring, and serving.
segments.thought_prompt: Design a feed ranking pipeline for 50M users with 500 candidate posts each. What's your end-to-end architecture?

segments.text: Feed ranking is a multi-stage ML pipeline: generate candidates, score with a learned model, apply diversity rules, and serve. Real-time push uses WebSockets with fan-out optimizations for high-follower accounts. Content moderation gates the write path. And Snowflake IDs provide distributed, time-sortable identifiers without coordination overhead.
